The GWAS of breed-average body weight recovered established body-size loci, confirming that the cohort could detect known associations. Of the 69 breed-weight loci, 30 were shared with breed-median lifespan, and at all of them the allele increasing body weight was associated with shorter lifespan. At the individual level, age at death, with breed-average body weight as a covariate, identified loci distinct from all breed-level loci. Three of them, the CDH4, TSHZ3 and TSC22D2 loci, replicated in the GRLS replication cohort. In humans, CDH4 and TSHZ3 have been implicated in longevity, and the region orthologous to the TSC22D2 locus has been associated with markers of biological ageing. Together, these results identify genetic variation associated with the lifespan of individual dogs beyond breed body size, and support the dog as a model in which genetic leads on ageing can be identified.

papers.title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.766027 v1

summary.background:
- GWAS (genome-wide association studies) find DNA variants statistically linked to traits or diseases; "fine-mapping" narrows these to the most likely causal variants.
- Noncoding variants sit outside protein-coding genes but can still change gene regulation.
- Chromatin accessibility: how tightly DNA is packed; open regions are usually where genes are switched on.
- Sequence-to-function models: machine-learning models that predict molecular activity from DNA sequence.
- Hematopoiesis: the process by which blood stem cells develop into mature blood cell types.
- CRISPRi: a method that silences a DNA region to test which genes it controls; K562 is a common leukemia-derived cell line used for this.
- CTCF motifs: short DNA sequences tied to the protein CTCF, which helps organize chromosome structure.
summary.one_liner: ChromBPNet deep-learning models trained on 17 hematopoietic cell types score about 303,000 noncoding variants for predicted effects on chromatin accessibility, and the paper compares these predictions with GWAS fine-mapping and K562 CRISPRi target-gene data.
summary.plain: Most disease-linked changes in human DNA fall in noncoding regions that do not code for proteins, so it is often unclear what they do. This paper uses computer models trained to predict how DNA changes affect how open or accessible genome regions are in blood cell types. The authors found that predicted effects follow the family tree of blood cell types, and that these predictions point to different variants than standard statistical gene-mapping methods do.
summary.why: It offers a cell-type-specific way to guess where noncoding disease variants act, which matters because most GWAS hits are noncoding. The text also states that the predictions say little about which genes these variants regulate, which limits how far they can be used on their own; the public prediction resource may be useful to others.

papers.abstract: Background. Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.

papers.title: Improved long-read sequencing technology reveals full genome architecture of Malian Plasmodium falciparum field isolates
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766388 v1

summary.background:
- Plasmodium falciparum is the parasite that causes the deadliest form of malaria.
- A reference genome is a complete reference copy of an organism's DNA, which other studies compare against.
- Long-read sequencing reads DNA in long pieces, which helps resolve repeated regions that short reads cannot place reliably.
- PacBio HiFi is a long-read technology that produces highly accurate reads.
- Contigs are continuous stretches of assembled DNA; fewer contigs means a more complete assembly.
- Subtelomeric and telomeric regions sit at chromosome ends; multigene families are groups of similar, repeated genes.
- Liftoff is a tool that transfers gene annotations (gene labels) from one genome to another.
- Cloned isolates come from a single parasite lineage, which avoids mixed-strain infections.
summary.one_liner: A de novo assembly strategy using PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing, applied to eight recently isolated and cloned Malian Plasmodium falciparum parasites, yields near-complete chromosomes and reveals variation in telomere and subtelomeric architecture and multicopy gene families.
summary.plain: Malaria parasites are hard to read genetically because their DNA is very rich in A and T letters and contains many repeated stretches, and most reference genomes come from lab-adapted strains that may not reflect parasites in the field. The authors tested a long-read sequencing method on eight parasites freshly collected from patients in Mali and found it could rebuild their genomes with few gaps, including the chromosome ends. The team reports that the chromosome ends and repeated gene families differed between these parasites.
summary.why: Better reference genomes from real field parasites can support studies of how malaria parasites vary and adapt across regions. The text reports a fourfold reduction in sequencing requirements, but its wider impact on malaria research is not established from this description alone.

papers.abstract: Understanding genome plasticity in malaria parasites and the diversity of their repetitive gene families requires high-quality reference genomes derived from parasites recently isolated from patients. However, generating such genomes in Plasmodium falciparum remains challenging owing to the parasite's extreme AT content, extensive repetitive regions, and the frequent occurrence of multiclonal infections in endemic settings. As a result, most available reference genomes are derived from laboratory-adapted strains, that have experienced prolonged in vitro maintenance, and that incompletely represent natural parasite diversity. We developed and optimized a de novo assembly strategy based on PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing and applied it to eight recently-isolated and cloned P. falciparum parasites from Mali. HiFi sequencing enabled highly accurate genome reconstruction, yielding assemblies with a mean of 18 contigs, 301 pseudogenes, and a frameshift rate of 0.04% following Liftoff annotation. Assemblies showed high structural integrity and near-complete chromosomes, including improved recovery of subtelomeric regions and multigene families, without requiring short-read correction. Despite overall conservation of chromosome organization, substantial variation was observed in chromosome-end architecture, subtelomeric structure, and telomeric repeat content among parasite genomes. Our approach simplifies the generation of high-quality P. falciparum genomes and reduces sequencing requirements fourfold. The resulting assemblies enabled characterization of natural variation in telomere plasticity and multicopy gene family diversity in field isolates. These findings establish PacBio HiFi sequencing as an effective and scalable strategy for producing highly contiguous and accurate de novo assemblies of P. falciparum, supporting the development of geographically-diverse, field-relevant malaria parasite reference genomes.
